title: Exciting Sports
pages: Book p.50 to 59 · Workbook p.40 to 47

learn.title: Welcome to Unit 5: Exciting Sports!
lines: In this unit you will:
🏂 learn words for extreme sports and safety equipment
⏳ use the present perfect with for and since
💥 make adjectives stronger with so, very, really, extremely
🎵 sing a song, 📖 read about brave athletes, 🌳 connect with nature, ✍️ write a biography

learn.title: Look at the big photo
lines: Open your book to pages 50 and 51.
A man is in a small green boat called a kayak. He is going down a big waterfall!
The photo is from Amazonas, Brazil.
This sport is called kayaking. It is an extreme sport: exciting and dangerous.

learn.title: How does he feel?
lines: We can describe feelings with a strong word before the adjective.
examples: He feels really happy.
He feels very worried.
He feels totally excited.
learn.note: You will learn more about really, very and totally in Grammar 2.

book.q: How do you think this person feels? Really happy, very worried, or totally excited?
book.answer: I think he feels totally excited.
book.hint: Look at his face and the big waterfall. Start with: I think he feels…

book.q: Would you ever do this sport?
book.answer: Yes, I would! It looks super exciting. / No, I wouldn't. It looks extremely dangerous.
book.hint: Answer Yes, I would or No, I wouldn't. Then give a reason.

book.q: Write a caption for the photo.
book.answer: Down the waterfall: totally exciting!
book.hint: A caption is a short title for a photo. Use only a few words.

models: This sport looks really exciting.
I think he feels totally excited.
Would you ever go kayaking?

turns.q: What is your favorite sport?
turns.example: My favorite sport is badminton.

turns.q: Would you ever go kayaking down a waterfall?
turns.starter: Yes, I would. / No, I wouldn't, because…
turns.example: No, I wouldn't, because it looks very dangerous!

sections.title: Vocabulary 1: Extreme Sports
sections.pages: Book p.52 to 53 · Workbook p.40 to 41

learn.title: What are extreme sports?
lines: Extreme sports are dangerous and exciting.
🪂 In the air: hang-gliding
🌊 In the water: kitesurfing
🚲 On land: BMX biking, skiing

learn.title: The text on page 52 (short summary)
lines: Read the full text in your book. Here is a short summary.
⛷️ Extreme skiers go super fast (240 km an hour) and fly a long way before they land.
🚲 In skiing and BMX biking, people flip in the air.
🌊 Kitesurfers travel across the water at 55 km an hour or more. They need strong arms. People call them "Charlie Browners."
🪂 Hang-gliders can fly like birds, as high as 6,000 m.
⚠️ Bad accidents are not common, but sometimes people get injuries.

learn.title: long → length, strong → strength, high → height
lines: Some adjectives have a noun partner.
examples: The bike is very long. What is its length?
The boy is strong. He has a lot of strength.
The hill is very high. What is its height?
table: strength ความแข็งแรง

learn.title: Actions: fly, flip, land, crash, travel
lines: These verbs describe what athletes do.
examples: The rider flipped in the air and landed safely.
James crashed into a tree, but he was OK.
learn.note: American spelling: traveled (one l), like in your book.

sections.title: Grammar 1: Present perfect with for and since

learn.title: The present perfect: from the past up to now
lines: We use the present perfect for something that started in the past and is still true now.
examples: I have lived here for ten years. (I still live here.)
Kitesurfing has been popular since 2000.

learn.title: How to make it: have / has + past participle
lines: I, you, we, they → have ('ve)
he, she, it, one sport → has ('s)
Not: haven't = have not, hasn't = has not

learn.title: FOR + a period of time ⏳
lines: Use for to say HOW LONG.
for ten years · for five days · for a month · for an hour · for a long time
examples: Surfing has been my favorite sport for many years.
Lily has had her bike for three years.
learn.note: Ask: Can I count it? (ten years, two weeks) → for

learn.title: SINCE + a point in time 📍
lines: Use since to say WHEN it started.
since 2016 · since June · since Monday · since last year · since the 1970s · since I was born
examples: Many people have had accidents since last year.
He has wanted to go skiing since he was a boy.
learn.note: Ask: Is it a start date or moment? (2016, Monday, I was born) → since

learn.title: Past participles you need
lines: Regular verbs add -ed. Irregular verbs change. Learn them!

learn.title: Asking: How long have you…?
lines: How long + have/has + person + past participle?
examples: How long have you had a bicycle?
I've had a bike for five years.
I've had one since I was six.

learn.title: Change since to for: do the math!
lines: Count the years from the start until now (2026).
examples: since 2014 → 2026 minus 2014 = 12 → for 12 years
since 2000 → 2026 minus 2000 = 26 → for 26 years
learn.note: Your workbook was written some years ago, so its example says "more than six years." Use this year for your answers.

book.q: Kitesurfing ____ popular for/since I was a kid.
book.inst: Use the words in the box. Write the verb, then underline for or since.
book.answer: Kitesurfing has been popular since I was a kid.
book.why: This is the example. "I was a kid" is a point in time, so since.

book.q: Surfing ____ my favorite sport for/since many years.
book.answer: Surfing has been my favorite sport for many years.
book.hint: Surfing = it, so use has. "Many years" is a period of time.
book.why: be → has been. Many years = how long → for.

book.q: Many people ____ accidents for/since last year.
book.answer: Many people have had accidents since last year.
book.hint: Many people = they, so use have. Which verb from the box goes with accidents?
book.why: have → have had. Last year = when it started → since.

book.q: Skiing ____ my dad's favorite sport for/since the last twenty years.
book.answer: Skiing has been my dad's favorite sport for the last twenty years.
book.hint: "The last twenty years" is how long.
book.why: be → has been. Twenty years = a period of time → for.

book.q: He ____ to go skiing for/since he was a boy.
book.answer: He has wanted to go skiing since he was a boy.
book.hint: Only "want" is left in the box. He → has.
book.why: want → has wanted. "He was a boy" is a point in time → since.

book.q: Use the game board in the back of the book. Take turns. Ask the person on your left a question.
book.answer: How long have you had a bicycle? I've had one for three years.
book.hint: Heads = move 1 space. Tails = move 2 spaces. Ask: How long have you…?

wb.q: My friends / be / fans of hang-gliding / 2014.
wb.inst: Look at the timeline. Write the sentences with since.
wb.answer: My friends have been fans of hang-gliding since 2014.
wb.why: This is the example in the workbook.

wb.q: People / enjoy / kitesurfing / 2000.
wb.answer: People have enjoyed kitesurfing since 2000.
steps: 2000 is a point in time → since.

wb.q: Surfing / be popular / around the world / the 1970s.
wb.answer: Surfing has been popular around the world since the 1970s.
steps: the 1970s is a point in time → since.

wb.q: 1960s / more than 10 million people / try / skateboarding.
wb.answer: More than 10 million people have tried skateboarding since the 1960s.
wb.hint: Start with the people. try → tried (y changes to i).

wb.q: Rewrite sentence 1 with for: My friends have been fans of hang-gliding since 2014.
wb.inst: Read the sentences in Activity 1 and do the math! Rewrite the sentences.
wb.answer: My friends have been fans of hang-gliding for 12 years.
wb.why: The workbook example says "for more than six years" because the book is older. In 2026 it is 12 years.

wb.q: Rewrite sentence 2 with for: People have enjoyed kitesurfing since 2000.
wb.answer: People have enjoyed kitesurfing for 26 years.

wb.q: Rewrite sentence 3 with for: Surfing has been popular around the world since the 1970s.
wb.answer: Surfing has been popular around the world for about 50 years.
steps: 2026 minus 1970 = 56, and 2026 minus 1979 = 47. So about 50 years.

wb.q: Rewrite sentence 4 with for: More than 10 million people have tried skateboarding since the 1960s.
wb.answer: More than 10 million people have tried skateboarding for more than 50 years.

sections.title: Grammar 2: Adverbs of emphasis

learn.title: Make adjectives stronger 💥
lines: Put so, very, really, incredibly, extremely, super, totally before an adjective.
cool → super cool 😎
examples: Skateboarding is so cool.
That trick is really scary.
Those knee pads look super silly.
This boy's helmet looks totally cool.

learn.title: Where does it go?
lines: Pattern: is / are / looks / seems + adverb + adjective
learn.note: ✗ Skateboarding is cool really. ✓ Skateboarding is really cool.

learn.title: Adjectives to use
table: น่าตื่นเต้น

learn.title: Giving opinions
lines: Start with I think (that)… Your friend can agree or disagree.
examples: I think that skateboarding is incredibly easy.
That's interesting. I think it's really difficult!
This sport looks extremely dangerous.
That's true. But it's totally cool!

learn.title: Danny MacAskill 🚲
lines: Read the full text "Cool Adventurers" in your book. This is a short summary.
Danny MacAskill is a famous extreme cyclist.
He flips off buildings and rides on trains with his bike!
He has crashed many times, but he is very lucky. He has only broken a few bones and twelve helmets.

learn.title: Bethany Hamilton 🏄‍♀️
lines: Bethany Hamilton is a surfer. She was born in Hawaii.
She was an extremely good surfer at the age of eight.
When she was 13, a shark attacked her and she lost her left arm.
One month later, she was back in the water! Since then, she has learned to surf with one arm and won competitions.

learn.title: Brave → braver, cool → cooler, lucky → luckier
lines: To compare two people, add -er to short adjectives.
brave → braver · cool → cooler · lucky → luckier (y → ier)
examples: I think Danny is braver because he performs really dangerous tricks.
But Bethany started surfing one month after her accident. That's incredibly brave!

learn.title: Low risk or high risk?
lines: Risk = the chance that something bad can happen.
Low risk: skateboarding, cycling

High risk: kitesurfing, extreme cycling

learn.title: An Extra Challenge (Workbook p.46)
lines: Read the full text in your workbook. This is a short summary.
Some athletes cannot see or hear, or have lost an arm or a leg. To do extreme sports, they need a lot of courage.

learn.title: High Climber: Matt Moniz (short summary)
lines: Read the full biography in your workbook. 📒
In 2007, Matt's father invited him to climb Mount Everest. He loved it!
The next year, he climbed Kilimanjaro in Africa and Elbrus in Russia.
In 2015, an earthquake caused an avalanche on Everest. Matt helped rescue injured climbers and won an award.
After that, he stayed in Nepal for a month to help rebuild schools and homes.

learn.title: Plan your biography
lines: 1. Who is the person? What is their exciting job, sport or trip?
2. When and how did it start?
3. What happened next? (then, the next year, suddenly)
4. What have they done since then? (since then + present perfect)

wb.q: Read the biography "High Climber." Underline the expressions that are used to link the events.
wb.answer: Before the age of nine · Then · suddenly · At the time · afterward · Since then · The next year · After that
wb.hint: There are 8 linking expressions. Look at the list of linking words at the top of the page.
steps: Paragraph 2 has one more, near the end.

wb.q: Write a short biography about someone who has an exciting job, does an exciting sport, or has traveled to exciting places. Link the events and dates.
wb.answer: Lily Evans is a rock climber. Before the age of ten, she only climbed trees. Then, in 2019, her uncle took her to a climbing wall. At the time, she was scared, but afterward she loved it. The next year, she climbed her first real mountain. Since then, she has won three competitions.
wb.hint: Use the plan in Learn. Use at least four linking words.
